## Use the identity in reverse {#iv5-using-magnitude-identity .vector-lesson .magnitude-lesson .geometric-lesson}

To work algebraically with magnitudes, rewrite a **squared magnitude** as a scalar product.

<div class="g-rule"><span data-math="|\underset{\sim}{a}|^2=\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}"></span></div>

<div class="g-magnitude-expansion">
<h3>The vector can be a difference, too</h3>
<div class="m-equation"><span data-math="\begin{aligned}|\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}|^2&=(\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a})\cdot(\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a})\\&=\underset{\sim}{b}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}-2\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{b}+\underset{\sim}{a}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}\end{aligned}"></span></div>
<p class="g-distributive-note">The last step uses the <strong>distributive property</strong> of the scalar product, which you will study in <strong>Extension 2</strong>.</p>
</div>

If a problem involves $|\underset{\sim}{a}|$ or $|\underset{\sim}{b}-\underset{\sim}{a}|$, working with its **square** lets us remove the magnitude signs and use scalar-product algebra.

::: notes
Emphasise the commonly useful direction |v|²=v·v, not only v·v=|v|². In the second example v=b−a. The expansion previews the distributive property, which students have not yet studied and will cover in Extension 2. The visible note explicitly acknowledges this; do not treat distributivity as assumed prior knowledge. The two cross terms are combined using commutativity. If the actual length is required, take the non-negative square root at the end; |v| itself is not v·v. This is a strategy for manipulating magnitudes, not an automatic instruction to square every equation (squaring can introduce extra solutions).
:::
